footerPosts.title: ACID Properties Explained: How SQL Databases Guarantee Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability
footerPosts.subtitle: A deep dive into PostgreSQL WAL logs, MVCC snapshot isolation, Write Skew anomalies, and crash recovery
footerPosts.brief: Trace how storage engines process high-stakes financial transactions like bank transfers using Write-Ahead Logging (WAL), Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC), and SSI locks without data loss or corruption.

footerPosts.title: ACID Transactions in Distributed Databases: DynamoDB, Cosmos DB, and Spanner Compared
footerPosts.subtitle: How modern NoSQL databases achieve atomicity and isolation without a single machine
footerPosts.brief: ACID transactions in distributed databases are not equal. DynamoDB provides multi-item atomicity scoped to 25 items using two-phase commit with a coordinator item, but only within a single region. Cosmos DB wraps partition-scoped operations inside a stored procedure using a JavaScript continuation model — cross-partition writes get no atomic guarantee. Google Spanner is the only cloud database that delivers true global ACID with external consistency, using TrueTime (GPS + atomic clocks) to assign globally ordered timestamps and a commit-wait delay to guarantee causality across datacenters. MongoDB supports multi-document transactions on replica sets but carries measurable performance overhead and does not prevent write skew under snapshot isolation. The right choice depends on atomicity scope, latency tolerance, and operational cost — not on which database claims to be "ACID-compliant."

footerPosts.title: Adapting to Virtual Threads for Spring Developers
footerPosts.subtitle: Migrate your Spring Boot services from thread-pool exhaustion to JDK 21 virtual threads — the practical Spring developer guide
footerPosts.brief: Platform threads (one OS thread per request) max out at a few hundred concurrent I/O-bound requests. Virtual threads (JDK 21+) allow millions — with zero I/O-blocking cost. Spring Boot 3.2 enables them with a single property. Avoid `synchronized` blocks wrapping I/O (they pin virtual threads to OS threads) and CPU-bound work inside virtual threads. For I/O-heavy Spring services, virtual threads are the most impactful JVM upgrade since Java 8 lambdas.

footerPosts.title: Advanced AI: Agents, RAG, and the Future of Intelligence
footerPosts.subtitle: Is an LLM a brain in a jar? To make it truly useful, we need to give it access to the world. This guide explains RAG and Agents.
footerPosts.brief: Large Language Models are brilliant "brains in a jar." Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) hands them a constantly refreshed memory, while AI Agents give them tools to act in the world. Combined, they turn static knowledge into dynamic, goal-directed intelligence — the next frontier of practical AI.

footerPosts.title: Advanced Graph Algorithms: Dijkstra, Topological Sort, and Disjoint Set Union (DSU)
footerPosts.subtitle: Master shortest paths, dependency resolution, and cycle detection with robust Java solutions.
footerPosts.brief: Graph algorithms are the backbone of networking, scheduling, and connection analysis. This guide explores Dijkstra's pathfinding, Topological Sorting for dependency resolution, and Disjoint Set Union (DSU) for cycle detection, complete with runnable Java code.

footerPosts.title: AI Agents Explained: When LLMs Start Using Tools
footerPosts.subtitle: An LLM can talk, but an AI Agent can *act*. We explain how Agents use the ReAct framework to brow...
footerPosts.brief: A standard LLM is a brain in a jar — it can reason but cannot act. An **AI Agent** connects that brain to tools (web search, code execution, APIs). Instead of just answering a question, an agent executes a loop of Thought → Action → Observation until the goal is reached.

footerPosts.title: AI Architecture Patterns: Routers, Planner-Worker Loops, Memory Layers, and Evaluation Guardrails
footerPosts.subtitle: Production AI needs explicit routing, memory, execution, and evaluation layers rather than one loop.
footerPosts.brief: A single agent loop is enough for a demo, but production AI systems need explicit layers for routing, execution, memory, and evaluation. Those layers determine safety, latency, cost, and traceability far more than model choice alone.

footerPosts.title: ANN Index Types Explained: When to Choose Flat, HNSW, IVF, or IVF-PQ
footerPosts.subtitle: A production-first guide to picking the right vector index for recall, latency, memory, and update patterns.
footerPosts.brief: If your dataset is small and correctness is critical, use Flat. If you need high recall with low latency and enough RAM, use HNSW. If your corpus is huge and memory is your bottleneck, use IVF-PQ. Start with HNSW for most RAG systems, then move to IVF or IVF-PQ when scale and cost force compression.

footerPosts.title: Apache Spark for Data Engineers: RDDs, DataFrames, and Structured Streaming
footerPosts.subtitle: Process petabytes with Python: understand Spark's execution model, DataFrame transformations, partitioning strategy, and real-time streaming.
footerPosts.brief: Apache Spark distributes Python DataFrame jobs across a cluster of executors, using lazy evaluation and the Catalyst query optimizer to process terabytes with the same code that works on gigabytes. Master partitioning, shuffle-awareness, and Structured Streaming and you have a single engine for both batch and real-time pipelines.

footerPosts.title: API Gateway vs. Load Balancer vs. Reverse Proxy: What's the Difference?
footerPosts.subtitle: They all sit in front of your servers. But do you need Nginx, HAProxy, or Kong? We clarify the roles of each component.
footerPosts.brief: A **Reverse Proxy** hides your servers and handles caching/SSL. A **Load Balancer** spreads traffic across server instances. An **API Gateway** manages API concerns — auth, rate limiting, routing, and protocol translation. Modern tools (Nginx, AWS ALB, Kong) often combine all three, but understanding what each layer does independently is essential for system design.

footerPosts.title: Attention Mechanism Explained: How Transformers Learn to Focus
footerPosts.subtitle: From the query-key-value formulation to multi-head attention — the mechanism that made transformers dominate AI
footerPosts.brief: Attention lets every token in a sequence ask "what else is relevant to me?" — dynamically weighting relationships across all positions simultaneously. It replaced the fixed-size hidden-state bottleneck of RNNs and is the engine behind every GPT, BERT, ViT, and AlphaFold model you have ever used.

footerPosts.title: Backend for Frontend (BFF): Tailoring APIs for UI
footerPosts.subtitle: Mobile apps need less data than Desktop dashboards. Why serve them the same JSON? The Backend for Frontend (BFF) pattern solves this.
footerPosts.brief: A "one-size-fits-all" API causes bloated mobile payloads and underpowered desktop dashboards. The **Backend for Frontend (BFF)** pattern solves this by creating a dedicated API server for each client type — the mobile BFF reshapes data for small screens, the web BFF aggregates for dashboards.

footerPosts.title: Exploring Backtracking Techniques in Data Structures
footerPosts.subtitle: Backtracking is a brute-force algorithmic technique that solves problems by trying to build a sol...
footerPosts.brief: Backtracking is "Recursion with Undo." You try a path, explore it deeply, and if it fails, you **undo** your last decision and try the next option. It explores the full search space but prunes invalid branches early, making it far more efficient than brute force.

footerPosts.title: BASE Theorem Explained: How it Stands Against ACID
footerPosts.subtitle: ACID guarantees consistency. BASE guarantees availability. We explain the trade-offs between SQL...
footerPosts.brief:
TLDR

TLDR: ACID (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability) is the gold standard for banking. BASE (Basically Available, Soft state, Eventual consistency) is the standard for social media. BASE i

footerPosts.title: BFS — Breadth-First Search: Level-by-Level Graph Exploration
footerPosts.subtitle: BFS explores graphs level by level using a queue — the key to shortest paths and level-order problems.
footerPosts.brief: BFS explores a graph level by level using a FIFO queue, guaranteeing the shortest path in unweighted graphs. Recognize BFS problems by keywords: "shortest path," "minimum steps," or "level order." Time: O(V + E). Space: O(V). Mark nodes visited on enqueue — never on dequeue.

footerPosts.title: Big Data 101: The 5 Vs, Ecosystem, and Why Scale Breaks Everything
footerPosts.subtitle: Why traditional databases fail at scale, what the 5 Vs really mean, and a practical map of the big data ecosystem from ingestion to insights.
footerPosts.brief: Traditional databases fail at big data scale for three concrete reasons — storage saturation, compute bottleneck, and write-lock contention. The 5 Vs (Volume, Velocity, Variety, Veracity, Value) frame what makes data "big." A layered ecosystem — Kafka for ingestion, S3 for storage, Spark for processing, Snowflake for serving — assigns one tool per failure mode.

footerPosts.title: Big Data Architecture Patterns: Lambda, Kappa, CDC, Medallion, and Data Mesh
footerPosts.subtitle: Choose ingestion, serving, and ownership patterns deliberately when data platforms start to scale.
footerPosts.brief: A serious data platform is defined less by where files are stored and more by how changes enter the system, how serving layers are materialized, and who owns quality over time. Lambda, Kappa, CDC, Medallion, and Data Mesh are patterns for making those choices explicit.

footerPosts.title: Big O Notation Explained: Time Complexity, Space Complexity, and Why They Matter in Interviews
footerPosts.subtitle: Master Big O notation: measure algorithm efficiency from O(1) to O(n²) with growth diagrams, worked examples, and the interview mental model.
footerPosts.brief: Big O notation describes how an algorithm's resource usage *grows* as input size grows — not how fast it runs on your laptop. Learn to identify the 7 complexity classes (O(1) through O(n!)), derive time and space complexity by counting loops and stack frames, and communicate your analysis in three sentences that satisfy any FAANG interviewer.

footerPosts.title: Binary Search Patterns: Five Variants Every Senior Engineer Knows
footerPosts.subtitle: Binary search has five distinct patterns — classic, leftmost, rightmost, rotated arrays, and 2D matrices.
footerPosts.brief: Binary search has five patterns beyond the classic "find the target": leftmost position, rightmost position, rotated array search, minimum in rotated array, and 2D matrix search. The root of every off-by-one bug is a mismatched loop condition and boundary update. Learn the invariant for each pattern and you will never write a broken binary search again.

footerPosts.title: Exploring Different Types of Binary Trees
footerPosts.subtitle: Not all Binary Trees are created equal. We explain Full, Complete, Perfect, and Balanced Binary T...
footerPosts.brief: A Binary Tree has at most 2 children per node, but the **shape** of the tree determines performance. A **Full** tree has 0 or 2 children. A **Complete** tree fills left-to-right. A **Perfect** tree is a symmetric triangle. A **Degenerate** tree becomes a linked list with $O(N)$ search.

articles.contentMarkdown:
## Scenario context

You're building an order service. The first version looks like this:

```architecture
{
  "version": 1,
  "title": "The Tightly Coupled Trap: When Changing a Database Breaks Business Logic - Storage Topology",
  "description": "Multi-tier caching and replicated storage pipeline ensuring fast reads and transactional consistency.",
  "view": "data-flow",
  "pattern": "cache-aside",
  "direction": "LR",
  "groups": […

Before making a design choice, clarify:

- You're building an order service.
- The first version looks like this: Six months later, you migrate to PostgreSQL.
- You search for every place MySQLDatabase() is used — it's woven through your order logic, your billing logic, your reporting.

**Concepts in play:** design-principles-solid, caching, jvm-internals-and-garbage-collection, consistency-replication

## Stage 1 — The Two Rules of Dependency Inversion

- The Dependency Inversion Principle has exactly two rules: 1.
- High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules.
- Both should depend on abstractions.
- Abstractions should not depend on details.

*Applies **design-principles-solid** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Abstractions should not depend on details.

## Stage 2 — The Principle: Abstractions Own the Contract

- The Dependency Inversion Principle has two parts: 1.
- High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules.
- Both should depend on abstractions.
- Abstractions should not depend on details.

*Applies **caching** to the decision above.*

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph Before DIP
        Biz1[OrderService] --> MySQL[MySQLDatabase]
        Biz1 --> Email1[SendGridClient]
    end
    subgraph After DIP
        Biz2[OrderService] --> IRepo[IOrderRepository abstraction]
        Biz2 --> IEmail[IEmailService abstraction]
        IRepo --> MySQL2[MySQLRepository]
        IRepo --> PG[PostgresRepository]
        IEmail --> Email2[SendGridEmailService]
        IEmail --> Mock[MockEmailService]
    end
```

**Observable outcome:** Abstractions should not depend on details.

## Stage 3 — DIP Dependency Direction

- Without DIP, high-level modules point arrows at low-level modules.
- With DIP, both point at abstractions in the middle — the direction of dependency is inverted.
- Reading the diagram: In the "With DIP" half, every arrow points AT the interface (the abstraction), never away from it.
- OrderService knows nothing about MySQL or SendGrid — only about the interface contracts.

*Applies **jvm-internals-and-garbage-collection** to the decision above.*

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Without_DIP[Without DIP]
        A[OrderService] --> B[MySQLDatabase]
        A --> C[SendGridClient]
    end
    subgraph With_DIP[With DIP]
        D[OrderService] --> E[IOrderRepository]
        D --> F[IEmailService]
        G[MySQLRepository] --> E
        H[PostgresRepository] --> E
        I[SendGridEmailService] --> F
        J[MockEmailService] --> F
    end
```

**Observable outcome:** OrderService knows nothing about MySQL or SendGrid — only about the interface contracts.

## Stage 4 — The Interface as the Contract: Python and Java Examples

- Python (using ABC): Switch to Postgres: OrderService(PostgresOrderRepository()) .
- Java (using interface): 📊 DIP Correct Pattern: Both Layers Depend on the Abstraction This diagram shows the corrected DIP pattern: OrderService now points to the abstractions IOrderRepository and IEmailService rather t…
- Both MySQLOrderRepository and PostgresOrderRepository implement IOrderRepository from below, so swapping database engines requires zero changes to OrderService .
- MockEmailService implementing IEmailService is precisely what enables unit testing — tests inject the mock and verify behavior without sending real emails or touching a real database.

*Applies **consistency-replication** to the decision above.*

```python
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class IOrderRepository(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def save(self, order) -> None: ...

    @abstractmethod
    def find_by_id(self, order_id: str): ...

class MySQLOrderRepository(IOrderRepository):
    def save(self, order):
        # MySQL-specific implementation
        ...

class PostgresOrderRepository(IOrderRepository):
    def save(self, order):
        # Postgres-specific implementation
        ...

class OrderService:
    def __init__(self, repo: IOrderRepository):   # depends on interface
        self.repo = repo

    def place_order(self, order):
        self.repo.save(order)
```

```java
public interface IOrderRepository {
    void save(Order order);
    Order findById(String id);
}

public class OrderService {
    private final IOrderRepository repo;          // depends on interface

    public OrderService(IOrderRepository repo) {
        this.repo = repo;
    }

    public void placeOrder(Order order) {
        repo.save(order);
    }
}
```

**Observable outcome:** MockEmailService implementing IEmailService is precisely what enables unit testing — tests inject the mock and verify behavior without sending real emails or touching a real database.

## Stage 5 — Deep Dive: Dependency Injection at Runtime

- DIP says what to depend on (abstractions).
- Dependency Injection (DI) says how to supply the concrete implementation at runtime.
- Constructor injection is the simplest and most testable option for most cases.
- Testing benefit: With DIP, unit tests can inject a mock: No database needed to test business logic.

*Applies **design-principles-solid** to the decision above.*

```python
class FakeOrderRepository(IOrderRepository):
    def __init__(self):
        self.saved = []
    def save(self, order):
        self.saved.append(order)

def test_place_order():
    repo = FakeOrderRepository()
    svc = OrderService(repo)
    svc.place_order(Order(id="1"))
    assert len(repo.saved) == 1
```

**Observable outcome:** Testing benefit: With DIP, unit tests can inject a mock: No database needed to test business logic.

## Stage 6 — Real-World Application: DIP Across Systems

- Spring Boot example: Spring's @Autowired and @Repository / @Service annotations are DIP at the framework level.
- You declare @Autowired IUserRepository repo in a service, and Spring injects the appropriate implementation.
- Business logic never instantiates infrastructure classes directly.
- Hexagonal architecture (Ports and Adapters): This architecture pattern IS DIP at the system design level.

*Applies **caching** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Hexagonal architecture (Ports and Adapters): This architecture pattern IS DIP at the system design level.

## End-to-end outcome

After working through the stages, you should be able to explain:

- - DIP makes testing a first-class concern.
- When business logic depends on interfaces, every external dependency (DB, email, HTTP) can be swapped for a fake in tests.

## Alternatives considered

### Decision Guide

Decision Guide


## Failure and degraded modes

### Trade-offs & Failure Modes: When DIP Adds Complexity

- **Detection:** DIP is not always the right answer: A sign that DIP is applied incorrectly: your project has 40 interfaces, all of which have exactly one implementation.
- **User or operator impact:** DIP is not always the right answer: A sign that DIP is applied incorrectly: your project has 40 interfaces, all of which have exactly one implementation.

articles.contentMarkdown:
## Scenario context

Designing a Vending Machine is a classic low-level design interview problem that tests state-driven logic. By using the GoF State Pattern, we avoid nested conditional blocks and build a modular, thread-safe system in Java Spring Boot.

---

Imagine you are tasked with developing the control software for a next-generation office vending machine. The machine must accept coins of different denominations, track a dynami…

This walkthrough focuses on **Design Challenge: The Fragile Vending Machine**.

Before making a design choice, clarify:

- Imagine you are tasked with developing the control software for a next-generation office vending machine.
- The machine must accept coins of different denominations, track a dynamic inventory of snacks, validate user selections, dispense products, and return change.
- A naive approach might rely on nested conditional checks to manage the machine's state: This code is fragile.

**Concepts in play:** low-level-design-systems, design-principles-solid, jvm-internals-and-garbage-collection, api-gateway

## Stage 1 — Scope: Use Cases and System Actors

- Before drawing class structures, we must establish the system boundary and identify the core functional requirements.
- Customer: The primary user who inserts money, selects products, requests refunds, and collects snacks and change.
- Maintenance Technician: An administrative user who refills inventory, collects accumulated cash, and audits machine health.
- Core Functional Requirements (Use Cases) Insert Money: The Customer inserts coins of recognized denominations (Nickel, Dime, Quarter, Dollar).

*Applies **low-level-design-systems** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Core Functional Requirements (Use Cases) Insert Money: The Customer inserts coins of recognized denominations (Nickel, Dime, Quarter, Dollar).

## Stage 2 — Architectural Blueprint: Class Diagram

- The class diagram below maps the relationships between the main components of our vending machine design, detailing variables, methods, and interface dependencies.
- This class diagram illustrates the implementation of the State Pattern.
- The VendingMachine maintains a reference to a VendingState interface and delegates all actions to it.
- The four concrete state implementations— IdleState , HasMoneyState , DispensingState , and OutOfStockState —override these actions to execute state-specific logic and trigger transitions by calling VendingMachine.setCur…

*Applies **design-principles-solid** to the decision above.*

```mermaid
classDiagram
    VendingMachine "1" *-- "1" VendingState : delegates to
    VendingMachine "1" *-- "1" Inventory : manages
    VendingState <|.. IdleState : implements
    VendingState <|.. HasMoneyState : implements
    VendingState <|.. DispensingState : implements
    VendingState <|.. OutOfStockState : implements
    class VendingState {
        <<interface>>
        +insertCoin(VendingMachine machine, Coin coin) void
        +selectProduct(VendingMachine machine, String slotId) void
        +dispense(VendingMachine machine) void
        +refund(VendingMachine machine) void
    }
    class VendingMachine {
        -VendingState currentState
        -Inventory inventory
        -int balance
        +setCurrentState(VendingState state) void
        +insertCoin(Coin coin) void
        +selectProduct(String slotId) void
        +dispense() void
        +refund() void
    }
```

**Observable outcome:** The four concrete state implementations— IdleState , HasMoneyState , DispensingState , and OutOfStockState —override these actions to execute state-specific logic and trigger transitions by calling VendingMachine.setCur…

## Stage 3 — Core Mechanics: Mapping the OOP Pillars

- Our design leverages the four core pillars of Object-Oriented Programming to ensure structural integrity: Abstraction: The VendingState interface defines a boundary.
- It hides state-specific transition rules from the VendingMachine and the client.
- The client calls generic methods like insertCoin without knowing how the machine transitions internally.
- Encapsulation: The VendingMachine encapsulates its internal variables—such as balance , selectedSlot , and inventory —restricting direct manipulation.

*Applies **jvm-internals-and-garbage-collection** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Encapsulation: The VendingMachine encapsulates its internal variables—such as balance , selectedSlot , and inventory —restricting direct manipulation.

## Stage 4 — Deep Dive: SOLID Walkthrough and Concurrency

- Let us walk through how our architecture implements SOLID design principles and handles concurrency in production.
- The Internals of State-Driven Execution Our vending machine design enforces multiple SOLID principles to maintain high codebase maintainability: Single Responsibility Principle (SRP): Each concrete state class has a sin…
- For example, IdleState only handles the initial coin insertion, delegating product selection warnings back to the client.
- Open-Closed Principle (OCP): Introducing a new state (e.g., MaintenanceState or CardAuthorizationState ) only requires writing a new class that implements VendingState and updating the transitions.

*Applies **api-gateway** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Open-Closed Principle (OCP): Introducing a new state (e.g., MaintenanceState or CardAuthorizationState ) only requires writing a new class that implements VendingState and updating the transitions.

## Stage 5 — Visualizing State Transitions: The Vending Flow

- To understand how the machine behaves as the user interacts with it, we map the lifecycle of a transaction.
- The diagram below shows the paths between states based on trigger actions.
- This state transition flowchart maps the operational phases of the vending machine.
- The system begins in the Idle state.

*Applies **low-level-design-systems** to the decision above.*

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Idle([Idle State]) -->|insertCoin| HasMoney([Has Money State])
    HasMoney -->|insertCoin| HasMoney
    HasMoney -->|selectProduct - balance ok| Dispensing([Dispensing State])
    HasMoney -->|refund / cancel| Idle
    Dispensing -->|dispense completed| Idle
    Dispensing -->|dispense - empty| OutOfStock([Out of Stock State])
    OutOfStock -->|refund| Idle
```

**Observable outcome:** The system begins in the Idle state.

## Stage 6 — Real-World Endpoint: Spring REST API

- To expose our LLD simulation to the client, we implement a Spring Boot @RestController mapping endpoints to the VendingMachine singleton.
- This controller handles coin insertions, product selections, and cancel requests, executing state transitions concurrently inside Spring container threads.

*Applies **design-principles-solid** to the decision above.*

```java
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.*;

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/vending")
public class VendingMachineController {

    private final VendingMachine machine = new VendingMachine();

    @GetMapping("/status")
    public VendingStatus getStatus() {
        return new VendingStatus(machine.getBalance(), machine.getSelectedSlot());
    }

    @PostMapping("/insert")
    public String insertCoin(@RequestParam Coin coin) {
        machine.insertCoin(coin);
        return "Balance updated: " + machine.getBalance();
    }

    @PostMapping("/select")
    public String selectProduct(@RequestParam String slotId) {
        machine.selectProduct(slotId);
        return "Selection processed.";
    }

    @PostMapping("/refund")
    public String refund() {
        machine.refund();
        return "Refund complete.";
    }
}

class VendingStatus {
    private final int balance;
    private final String selectedSlot;

    public VendingStatus(int balance, String selectedSlot) {
        this.balance = balance;
        this.selectedSlot = selectedSlot;
    }
    public int getBalance() { return balance; }
    public String getSelectedSlot() { return selectedSlot; }
}
```

**Observable outcome:** This controller handles coin insertions, product selections, and cancel requests, executing state transitions concurrently inside Spring container threads.

## End-to-end outcome

After working through the stages, you should be able to explain:

- When designing state-driven LLD systems: 1.
- Keep Context Synchronized: Always declare context methods that alter mutable variables (like insertCoin , selectProduct ) as synchronized to ensure thread-safety in multi-threaded container environments.
- State Pattern: Encapsulates state-specific logic in dedicated classes, avoiding nested if-else structures.
- OOP Abstraction: Hides transition details completely behind interface contracts.

articles.contentMarkdown:
## Scenario context

You pull up to a mall garage. Three things happen:
1. **Entry gate:** You press a button → get a ticket → gate opens.
2. **Parking:** Find a spot (the system might display "Floor 2, Spot 14").
3. **Exit:** Scan your ticket → system calculates fee based on time parked → gate opens.

The software behind this manages hundreds of concurrent vehicles across multiple floors, spot types, and pricing tiers.

---

This walkthrough focuses on **The Mall Garage Problem**.

Before making a design choice, clarify:

- Entry gate: You press a button → get a ticket → gate opens.
- Parking: Find a spot (the system might display "Floor 2, Spot 14").
- Exit: Scan your ticket → system calculates fee based on time parked → gate opens.

**Concepts in play:** tree-data-structures, low-level-design-systems, vector-databases-rag, design-patterns-gof

## Stage 1 — Parking Lot Design Basics

- Before writing any code, it helps to map out the real-world entities the system must represent.
- Spot Types — Not every bay fits every vehicle.
- A typical garage divides its spaces into three tiers: Vehicle Types — Each vehicle carries a licensePlate and a VehicleType enum ( BIKE , CAR , TRUCK ).
- The type determines which spot tier it can occupy — a TRUCK cannot squeeze into a CompactSpot .

*Applies **tree-data-structures** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** The type determines which spot tier it can occupy — a TRUCK cannot squeeze into a CompactSpot .

## Stage 2 — The Domain Model

- Hierarchy: - ParkingSpot → subclasses: BikeSpot , CompactSpot , LargeSpot - Vehicle → subclasses: Bike , Car , Truck - ParkingLot → Singleton (one physical lot, one controller)

*Applies **low-level-design-systems** to the decision above.*

```mermaid
classDiagram

        -static ParkingLot instance
        +List~ParkingFloor~ floors
        -PricingStrategy pricingStrategy
        +Ticket park(Vehicle v)
        +double exit(Ticket t)
    }
    class ParkingFloor {
        +int floorNumber
        -Map~VehicleType,PriorityQueue~ heaps
        +ParkingSpot findNearest(VehicleType t)
        +void releaseSpot(ParkingSpot s)
    }
    class ParkingSpot {
        <<abstract>>
        +int id
        +boolean isFree
        +VehicleType type
        +void assign(Vehicle v)
        +void free()
    }
    class BikeSpot {
        +VehicleType type = BIKE
    }
    class CompactSpot {
        +VehicleType type = CAR
    }
    class LargeSpot {
        +VehicleType type = TRUCK
    }
    class Vehicle {
        <<abstract>>
        +String licensePlate
        +VehicleType type
    }
    class Bike
    class Car
    class Truck
    class Ticket {
        +Vehicle vehicle
        +ParkingSpot spot
        +Instant entryTime
    }
    class PricingStrategy {
        <<interface>>
        +calculateFee(VehicleType type, long minutes) double
    }
    class HourlyPricing {
        +calculateFee(VehicleType type, long minutes) double
    }

    ParkingLot "1" *-- "many" ParkingFloor : owns
    ParkingFloor "1" *-- "many" ParkingSpot : contains

    CompactSpot --|> ParkingSpot : extends

    Ticket --> Vehicle : records
    Ticket --> ParkingSpot : records

```

**Observable outcome:** Hierarchy: - ParkingSpot → subclasses: BikeSpot , CompactSpot , LargeSpot - Vehicle → subclasses: Bike , Car , Truck - ParkingLot → Singleton (one physical lot, one controller)

## Stage 3 — OOP Pillars in the Parking Lot Domain

- The four OOP pillars are not abstract ideals here — each one maps to a concrete class or interface in this design.
- Encapsulation — ParkingFloor hides its Min-Heap ParkingFloor owns a Map<VehicleType, PriorityQueue<ParkingSpot internally.
- No external class ever touches that map directly.
- The public surface is exactly two methods: findNearest(VehicleType) (wraps poll() ) and releaseSpot(ParkingSpot) (wraps offer() ).

*Applies **vector-databases-rag** to the decision above.*

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> AVAILABLE : spot added to Min-Heap
    AVAILABLE --> OCCUPIED : findNearest()  assign(vehicle)
    OCCUPIED --> AVAILABLE : releaseSpot()  re-insert into heap
    AVAILABLE --> [*] : floor decommissioned
```

**Observable outcome:** The public surface is exactly two methods: findNearest(VehicleType) (wraps poll() ) and releaseSpot(ParkingSpot) (wraps offer() ).

## Stage 4 — Finding the Nearest Spot: Min-Heap

- A naive O(N) linear scan through all spots is too slow for a large garage.
- Optimized: Use a Min-Heap (priority queue ordered by spot ID, lowest = nearest entrance) per vehicle type per floor.
- Operations: - findNearest(CAR) → heaps.get(CAR).poll() → O(log N) - releaseSpot(spot) → heaps.get(spot.type).offer(spot) → O(log N) For N = 1000 spots per floor: log₂(1000) ≈ 10 operations vs.

*Applies **design-patterns-gof** to the decision above.*

```
Floor 1 Compact Heap: [101, 103, 107, ...]   ← pop 101 in O(log N)
Floor 1 Large Heap:   [150, 155, ...]
```

**Observable outcome:** Operations: - findNearest(CAR) → heaps.get(CAR).poll() → O(log N) - releaseSpot(spot) → heaps.get(spot.type).offer(spot) → O(log N) For N = 1000 spots per floor: log₂(1000) ≈ 10 operations vs.

## Stage 5 — Deep Dive: Factory and Strategy Patterns

- Callers use VehicleFactory.create(VehicleType.CAR, "ABC-123") — never new Car(...) directly.
- This decouples object creation from business logic and makes it easy to add ElectricVehicle later.

*Applies **tree-data-structures** to the decision above.*

```java
public class VehicleFactory {
    public static Vehicle create(VehicleType type, String plate) {
        return switch (type) {
            case BIKE   -> new Bike(plate);
            case CAR    -> new Car(plate);
            case TRUCK  -> new Truck(plate);
        };
    }
}
```

**Observable outcome:** This decouples object creation from business logic and makes it easy to add ElectricVehicle later.

## Stage 6 — Strategy Pattern for Pricing

- Pricing rules vary (hourly, daily, weekend, EV charging surcharge): The ParkingLot holds a reference to any PricingStrategy .
- Swapping from HourlyPricing to DynamicPricing requires zero changes to the rest of the code.
- 📊 Factory and Strategy: Class Diagram This class diagram extends the core domain model to show the full Factory and Strategy pattern integration, including the VehicleFactory creation point, the pluggable PricingStrate…
- The key relationship is that ParkingLot depends on interfaces ( PricingStrategy , SpotAllocator ) rather than concrete classes, which is what allows EVSpot and ChargingPricing to be added without modifying any existing…

*Applies **low-level-design-systems** to the decision above.*

```java
public interface PricingStrategy {
    double calculateFee(VehicleType type, long parkingMinutes);
}

public class HourlyPricing implements PricingStrategy {
    public double calculateFee(VehicleType type, long minutes) {
        double ratePerHour = type == VehicleType.TRUCK ? 3.50 :
                             type == VehicleType.CAR   ? 2.00 : 1.00;
        return ratePerHour * Math.ceil(minutes / 60.0);
    }
}
```

```mermaid
classDiagram

        +create(VehicleType, String) Vehicle
    }

        <<interface>>
        +calculateFee(VehicleType, long) double
    }

    }

    }

        +findNearest(VehicleType, List~ParkingFloor~) Optional~ParkingSpot~
        +release(ParkingSpot, List~ParkingFloor~) void
    }

    }
    class ParkingLot {
        -PricingStrategy pricingStrategy
        -SpotAllocator allocator
        +park(Vehicle) Ticket
        +exit(Ticket) double
    }

    ParkingLot o-- PricingStrategy : uses (injected)
    ParkingLot o-- SpotAllocator : uses (injected)
    VehicleFactory --> Vehicle : creates
    EVSpot --|> ParkingSpot : extends
```

**Observable outcome:** The key relationship is that ParkingLot depends on interfaces ( PricingStrategy , SpotAllocator ) rather than concrete classes, which is what allows EVSpot and ChargingPricing to be added without modifying any existing…

## End-to-end outcome

Entry gate: You press a button → get a ticket → gate opens.

LLD for LRU Cache: Designing a High-Performance Cache
articles.contentMarkdown:
## Scenario context

A **cache** is a small, fast store that holds a hot subset of a larger, slower dataset. When your application repeatedly reads the same data from a database, remote API, or disk, caching the results in memory slashes latency from milliseconds to microseconds.

Because caches have limited capacity, they need an **eviction policy** — a rule for deciding which item to drop when the cache is full and a new item arrives.…

This walkthrough focuses on **Eviction Policies: Why LRU Makes Sense**.

Before making a design choice, clarify:

- A cache is a small, fast store that holds a hot subset of a larger, slower dataset.
- When your application repeatedly reads the same data from a database, remote API, or disk, caching the results in memory slashes latency from milliseconds to microseconds.
- Because caches have limited capacity, they need an eviction policy — a rule for deciding which item to drop when the cache is full and a new item arrives.

**Concepts in play:** caching, low-level-design-systems, hash-tables-and-bloom-filters, database-indexing

## Stage 1 — The Browser History Analogy

- Your browser "Back" button stores the pages you visited most recently.
- If you visit 100 pages and your browser only keeps 10 in memory, it drops the oldest one.
- LRU says: the item you haven't needed in the longest time is the least valuable — evict it first.
- The classic challenge is implementing this in O(1) for both get and put .

*Applies **caching** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** The classic challenge is implementing this in O(1) for both get and put .

## Stage 2 — The HashMap + Doubly Linked List Architecture

- architecture { "version": 1, "title": "The HashMap + Doubly Linked List Architecture - Subsystem Overview", "description": "Decoupled system architecture isolating ingress, stateless logic, and persistent datastores.",…
- Together, both get() and put() complete in O(1) — something neither data structure can achieve alone.
- The arrow represents the dependency: every cache operation starts at the HashMap to retrieve the node reference, then hands off to the DLL for order-preserving position updates.
- - HashMap: Maps each key to its Node in the list— O(1) access.

*Applies **low-level-design-systems** to the decision above.*

```mermaid

```

```

flowchart LR
    HashMap["HashMap (key  node pointer)"] --> DLL["Doubly Linked List Head (MRU)  ...  Tail (LRU)"]
```

**Observable outcome:** - HashMap: Maps each key to its Node in the list— O(1) access.

## Stage 3 — Step-by-Step Trace: Capacity = 3

- Key: get(1) bumped 1 to head, so 3 became the new tail.
- When 4 arrives, 2 gets evicted — not 3.
- 📊 Cache Entry Lifecycle States The state machine captures the complete lifecycle of a single cache entry from insertion to eviction.
- A node enters as HOT (placed at the head/MRU position) and returns to HOT whenever get() is called on it, resetting its eviction clock with each access.

*Applies **hash-tables-and-bloom-filters** to the decision above.*

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> HOT : put(key, val)  inserted at head (MRU)
    HOT --> HOT : get(key)  moved back to head
    HOT --> COLD : newer entries push it toward tail
    COLD --> HOT : get(key)  moved back to head (MRU)
    COLD --> EVICTED : cache full  tail node removed on next put()
    EVICTED --> [*]
```

**Observable outcome:** A node enters as HOT (placed at the head/MRU position) and returns to HOT whenever get() is called on it, resetting its eviction clock with each access.

## Stage 4 — LRU Cache Operation Flow

- Every get and put follows a deterministic decision path.
- Tracking which branch executes is the key to understanding unexpected evictions.
- This decision tree captures every execution path through get() and put() in a single view.
- The left branch ( get ) is two steps: a HashMap lookup, then either a miss (return -1) or a move-to-head followed by returning the value.

*Applies **database-indexing** to the decision above.*

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Request arrives] --> B{get or put?}
    B -->|"get(key)"| C{Key in HashMap?}
    C -->|No| D["Return -1 (cache miss)"]
    C -->|Yes| E["Move node to head (mark as MRU)"]
    E --> F["Return value (cache hit)"]
    B -->|"put(key, val)"| G{Key exists?}
    G -->|Yes| H[Update value Move node to head]
    G -->|No| I[Create new node Insert at head]
    I --> J{Size > capacity?}
    J -->|Yes| K[Remove tail node Delete from HashMap]
    J -->|No| L[Done ]
    K --> L
```

**Observable outcome:** The left branch ( get ) is two steps: a HashMap lookup, then either a miss (return -1) or a move-to-head followed by returning the value.

## Stage 5 — How the Four OOP Pillars Shape the LRU Cache Design

- Object-oriented design is not just syntax — it is a discipline for assigning clear, bounded responsibilities to each class.
- The LRU cache is a compact example of all four OOP pillars working together in a single design.
- Encapsulation: The Node<K,V inner class — with its prev and next pointers — is declared private static .
- A dedicated DoublyLinkedList helper manages all pointer manipulation.

*Applies **caching** to the decision above.*

```mermaid
classDiagram
    direction LR
    class Cache~K,V~ {
        <<interface>>
        +get(key K) Optional~V~
        +put(key K, value V) void
        +size() int
        +capacity() int
    }
    class LruCache~K,V~ {
        -capacity int
        -map HashMap
        -head Node
        -tail Node
        +get(key K) Optional~V~
        +put(key K, value V) void
    }
    class LfuCache~K,V~ {
        -capacity int
        -freqMap HashMap
        +get(key K) Optional~V~
        +put(key K, value V) void
    }
    class Node~K,V~ {
        -key K
        -value V
        -prev Node
        -next Node
    }
    Cache <|.. LruCache : implements
    Cache <|.. LfuCache : implements
    LruCache *-- Node : has-a (private)
```

**Observable outcome:** A dedicated DoublyLinkedList helper manages all pointer manipulation.

## Stage 6 — SOLID Principles in the LRU Cache Design

- Getting the algorithm right is only half the job in LLD.
- The other half is designing classes that are easy to extend, test, and replace independently.
- Every SOLID principle has a concrete mapping in the LRU cache design.
- SRP in practice: When a pointer-corruption bug surfaces, you look inside DoublyLinkedList .

*Applies **low-level-design-systems** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** SRP in practice: When a pointer-corruption bug surfaces, you look inside DoublyLinkedList .

## End-to-end outcome

A cache is a small, fast store that holds a hot subset of a larger, slower dataset.

## Alternatives considered

### Decision Guide: Choosing the Right Cache Implementation

Start with synchronized methods for correctness.


## Failure and degraded modes

### Trade-offs & Failure Modes: Thread Safety and Cache Invalidation

- **Detection:** The basic implementation above is not thread-safe.
- **User or operator impact:** The basic implementation above is not thread-safe.

articles.contentMarkdown:
## Scenario context

Building an in-memory message queue is a premier LLD problem testing multithreaded design. By combining the observer pattern with Java reentrant locks, conditions, and concurrent atomic offsets, we implement a thread-safe broker that decouples producers and consumers.

* * *

Imagine you are building an in-memory logging and analytics processing engine for a microservice. Different parts of the application (e.g., HT…

This walkthrough focuses on **Design Challenge: Thread Contention in Event-Driven Systems**.

Before making a design choice, clarify:

- Imagine you are building an in-memory logging and analytics processing engine for a microservice.
- Different parts of the application (e.g., HTTP request loggers, billing events, security auditors) generate messages that must be processed asynchronously by multiple worker threads.
- A naive observer pattern implementation couples the publisher and subscriber.

**Concepts in play:** low-level-design-systems, stack-and-queue-data-structures, jvm-internals-and-garbage-collection, message-queues

## Stage 1 — Scope: System Actors and Core Requirements

- Before implementing the class model, we establish the requirements for our in-memory queue and define how actors interact.
- System Actors Producer: Represents the client thread generating messages.
- It publishes events to specific topics.
- Consumer: An independent execution thread that continuously polls messages from specific topics and partitions.

*Applies **low-level-design-systems** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Consumer: An independent execution thread that continuously polls messages from specific topics and partitions.

## Stage 2 — Architectural Blueprint: Class Diagram

- The class diagram below outlines the structural composition of our in-memory queue: This class diagram details the relationships between the core components of our concurrent queue broker.
- The QueueBroker manages multiple Topic objects.
- Each Topic contains multiple TopicPartition structures.
- Each partition encapsulates a thread-safe array of Message entities, utilizing a ReentrantLock and a Condition variable to coordinate producers and consumers safely.

*Applies **stack-and-queue-data-structures** to the decision above.*

```mermaid
classDiagram
    QueueBroker "1" *-- "*" Topic : manages
    Topic "1" *-- "*" TopicPartition : contains
    TopicPartition "1" *-- "*" Message : holds
    ConsumerGroup "1" *-- "*" ConsumerInstance : coordinates
    ConsumerInstance --> QueueBroker : polls from
    class TopicPartition {
        -List~Message~ messages
        -ReentrantLock lock
        -Condition hasMessages
        +append(Message msg) void
        +read(int offset) Message
    }
    class ConsumerInstance {
        -String id
        -ConsumerGroup group
        +poll() void
    }
```

**Observable outcome:** Each partition encapsulates a thread-safe array of Message entities, utilizing a ReentrantLock and a Condition variable to coordinate producers and consumers safely.

## Stage 3 — Core Mechanics: Mapping the OOP Pillars

- Our design leverages the four pillars of Object-Oriented Programming to ensure clean separation of concerns: Abstraction: The QueueBroker abstracts partition management, offsets, and thread coordination.
- Producers simply call publish(topic, message) without managing lock states.
- The details of how messages are stored, indexed, and synchronized are completely hidden from the publisher.
- Encapsulation: The message list and read offsets are encapsulated inside TopicPartition and ConsumerGroup respectively.

*Applies **jvm-internals-and-garbage-collection** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Encapsulation: The message list and read offsets are encapsulated inside TopicPartition and ConsumerGroup respectively.

## Stage 4 — Deep Dive: Thread Synchronization and Consumer Offsets

- Let's look at the concurrency mechanics required to handle high-throughput message ingestion.
- The Internals of Lock-Free Offsets and Blocking Queues To guarantee thread-safety without creating bottlenecks, we isolate lock boundaries.
- If we locked the entire QueueBroker or Topic during a write, we would serialise all operations.
- Producers writing to unrelated topics would block each other.

*Applies **message-queues** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Producers writing to unrelated topics would block each other.

## Stage 5 — Visualizing Concurrency: The Producer-Consumer Flow

- The flowchart below visualizes the thread interaction between producers appending messages and consumers waiting for new data.
- This concurrency sequence diagram illustrates how producers and consumers synchronize.
- A consumer thread attempting to read from an empty partition enters a waiting state by calling await() on the partition's condition variable.
- When a producer thread locks the partition and appends a message, it invokes signal() .

*Applies **low-level-design-systems** to the decision above.*

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Producer[Producer Thread] -->|lock| Partition[Topic Partition]
    Partition -->|append message| MsgList[Message List]
    MsgList -->|signal hasMessages| Consumer[Consumer Thread]
    Consumer -->|await on hasMessages| Idle[Waiting State]
    MsgList -->|read message| Consumer
```

**Observable outcome:** When a producer thread locks the partition and appends a message, it invokes signal() .

## Stage 6 — Decision and Extension: Custom Partition Routing

- In production systems, routing messages to partitions depends on the use case.
- By introducing a routing abstraction, we can dynamically change routing behavior without modifying the broker class.
- We compare standard strategies below: Using a polymorphic RoutingStrategy allows the client to select the correct balancing behavior dynamically based on system demands.

*Applies **stack-and-queue-data-structures** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** We compare standard strategies below: Using a polymorphic RoutingStrategy allows the client to select the correct balancing behavior dynamically based on system demands.

## End-to-end outcome

After working through the stages, you should be able to explain:

- Keep these best practices in mind when designing multithreaded queues: 1.
- Avoid Global Locks: Place locks inside individual partitions rather than at the topic level to isolate lock contention.
- Partition Isolation: Place locks inside individual partitions to support concurrent parallel writes.
- Reentrant Locks: Use Java's ReentrantLock and Condition to block and wake up consumer threads safely.

## Alternatives considered

The source focuses on one primary design. A second architecture is not compared, so no alternative is invented here.

## Failure and degraded modes

### Trade-offs and Failure Modes: In-Memory Storage Limits

- **Detection:** Operating an event queue entirely in-memory introduces critical trade-offs: JVM Memory Pressure (Out of Memory): Since messages are stored inside Java lists, a slow consumer group will cause partitio…
- **User or operator impact:** Operating an event queue entirely in-memory introduces critical trade-offs: JVM Memory Pressure (Out of Memory): Since messages are stored inside Java lists, a slow consumer group will cause partitio…

This walkthrough focuses on **Why Base62 and Not MD5?**.

Before making a design choice, clarify:

- Approach A — Hashing (MD5/SHA): - Hash the long URL: MD5("https://...") = 3b94d2a8...
- - Take first 7 chars: 3b94d2a .
- - Problem: Two different URLs might produce the same first 7 chars → collision → wrong redirect.

**Concepts in play:** caching, design-patterns-gof, jvm-internals-and-garbage-collection, low-level-design-systems

## Stage 1 — The Locker Room Analogy

- A locker room assigns locker numbers.
- The attendant doesn't randomly pick numbers — she uses the next available sequential number.
- You get "Locker 5" → you can find it instantly.
- URL shorteners work the same way: assign a unique sequential integer ID , then encode it in a compact string format.

*Applies **caching** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** URL shorteners work the same way: assign a unique sequential integer ID , then encode it in a compact string format.

## Stage 2 — Short Codes, Redirects, and TTL: The Core Vocabulary

- Before building, align on the four concepts everything else depends on.
- Short Code — the compact identifier that replaces a long URL.
- cb , Xk3 , and my-blog are all short codes.
- They appear after the domain: https://tiny.url/cb .

*Applies **design-patterns-gof** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** They appear after the domain: https://tiny.url/cb .

## Stage 3 — OOP Contracts: Interfaces and Collaborations

- The URL shortener's backbone is four focused Java interfaces.
- Each defines a contract — an agreement about what a collaborator can do without revealing how it does it.
- UrlShortenerService holds a reference to each interface and receives them via constructor injection; it never references a concrete class directly.
- Who implements each interface, who calls it, and what it abstracts: Runtime collaboration — how the components interact during a shorten() call: Structural relationships — ownership and implementation: This class diagra…

*Applies **jvm-internals-and-garbage-collection** to the decision above.*

}

interface CodeStore {
    String save(String longUrl);            // stores mapping, returns short code
    Optional<String> resolve(String code);  // looks up long URL by short code
    boolean exists(String code);            // deduplication check
}

interface AnalyticsTracker {

}

interface AliasValidator {

```

## Stage 4 — OOP Pillars Applied to the URL Shortener

- Each classical OOP pillar maps directly to a concrete design decision in this system.
- Encapsulation — Base62Encoder owns its alphabet The 62-character alphabet ( a-z A-Z 0-9 ) and the modular-arithmetic encoding loop are private implementation details inside Base62Encoder .
- Callers invoke encode(125) and receive "cb" — they never see the CHARS constant or the while (id 0) loop.
- Swapping the alphabet (say, to a URL-safe Base64 variant) requires editing exactly one class, nowhere else.

*Applies **low-level-design-systems** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Swapping the alphabet (say, to a URL-safe Base64 variant) requires editing exactly one class, nowhere else.

## Stage 5 — SOLID Principles in the URL Shortener Design

- SOLID is not an abstract checklist — each principle appears as a specific, verifiable choice here.
- Single Responsibility (SRP) — Each class has exactly one reason to change.
- Base62Encoder changes only if the encoding algorithm changes.
- A CodeStore implementation changes only if the persistence technology changes.

*Applies **caching** to the decision above.*

```java
public class UrlShortenerService {
    private final UrlEncoder encoder;
    private final CodeStore store;
    private final AnalyticsTracker tracker;

    public UrlShortenerService(UrlEncoder encoder, CodeStore store, AnalyticsTracker tracker) {
        this.encoder = encoder;
        this.store   = store;
        this.tracker = tracker;
    }
}
```

**Observable outcome:** A CodeStore implementation changes only if the persistence technology changes.

## Stage 6 — Interface Contracts: The Four Boundaries of the URL Shortener

- Each interface is a stable boundary.
- Anything inside that boundary can change freely; anything outside can only call the methods listed here.
- These four contracts are everything UrlShortenerService needs from the outside world.
- Any Spring @Bean that satisfies an interface can be wired in — production configs, test configs, and migration configs all swap implementations without modifying the service itself.

*Applies **design-patterns-gof** to the decision above.*

```java
/**
 * Converts a numeric counter ID into a compact short-code string.
 * Implementations: Base62Encoder, CustomAliasEncoder, Base58Encoder
 */
interface UrlEncoder {
    String encode(long id);  // e.g. encode(125) → "cb"
}

/**
 * Persists and retrieves short-code ↔ long-URL mappings.
 * Implementations: InMemoryStore (test), RedisStore (staging), DistributedStore (prod)
 */
interface CodeStore {
    String save(String longUrl);            // persists mapping, returns generated short code
    Optional<String> resolve(String code);  // returns long URL for code, or empty if not found
    boolean exists(String code);            // returns true if the code is already in use
}

/**
 * Records analytics for every redirect event.
 * Implementations: NoOpTracker (default), DatabaseTracker (analytics-on)
 */
interface AnalyticsTracker {
    void recordClick(String code, String referrer, Instant timestamp);
}

/**
 * Validates user-supplied custom aliases before storage.
 * Implementations: CustomAliasValidator
 */
interface AliasValidator {
    boolean isValid(String customAlias);  // false if blank, reserved, non-alphanumeric, or taken
}
```
